reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes signing up for Coinbase through a referral link, promises both parties $10, and tells viewers to buy $100 of Bitcoin so the speaker receives a referral reward. The speaker also asks viewers to send Bitcoin, while the description supplies a Bitcoin address and the closing card pairs a send-Bitcoin instruction with a QR code. The Coinbase walkthrough and mocking accusations against the platform do not negate these referral and transfer requests.

buy $100 worth of bitcoin so I get my $10 referral

Send Bitcoin to: 1CvxqySazxycehpTwZTFacCqEAGy7dErLy

opening.argument: The presentation repeatedly warns viewers against Coinbase rather than presenting it as a safe or guaranteed way to profit. The speaker calls Coinbase “the biggest thieves in the world,” says users should read the agreement carefully, and expressly says that people who do not want to use Coinbase probably should not use it. Those are plainly cautionary signals, even if delivered through crude exaggeration and satire. The description also identifies the activity as a demonstration of how to use Coinbase, not a promise that viewers will receive a guaranteed return. The evidence therefore supports critical commentary and risk warning about a third-party service, rather than deceptive scam promotion.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The referral language is surrounded by explicit hostility toward Coinbase, including repeated claims that users will be harmed. A request to use a referral link does not erase the video's dominant warning and mocking treatment of the service. The transfer request also does not establish deception merely because an address is provided; its purpose and recipient context are not established by the cited material.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Warnings do not negate the concrete solicitation. The speaker tells viewers to sign up through the speaker's link, buy a specified amount, and send Bitcoin afterward. Calling Coinbase harmful can function as humor or commentary while the speaker still seeks the referral reward and cryptocurrency. The warning language does not show that the referral offer is merely investigative or that viewers are protected from loss.

opening.argument: The video's central activity is an operational walkthrough of Coinbase. It explains signing up, verifying an email, accepting terms, reviewing the dashboard, adding a payment method, and reaching the buy-and-sell function. The supplied frames corroborate that the presentation shows Coinbase's public landing page, sign-up screen, dashboard, and payment-method interface. The description directly characterizes the content as demonstrating how to use Coinbase to buy Bitcoin. A tutorial may mention an available referral feature without becoming a scam; the evidence establishes instruction about using a service, not a false investment claim or fabricated outcome.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited referral remarks occur within the same step-by-step explanation of how Coinbase works. They do not establish that the tutorial is fabricated, that Coinbase is falsely represented as safe, or that a viewer must pay the speaker. The frames show actual Coinbase account and payment interfaces, which is consistent with an operational demonstration rather than proof of a scam mechanism.

citations.quote: The Blockchain Boys demonstrate how to use Coinbase to buy Bitcoin and to earn Bitcoin by inviting friends

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Instructional format does not change the commercial call to action. The speaker does not merely explain that Coinbase has referrals; the speaker directs viewers to use the speaker's link, buy $100, and send the resulting Bitcoin. The tutorial's real screens establish that Coinbase exists, but they do not establish that the speaker's referral solicitation is harmless or that the promised reward was available.

citations.quote: sign up through my link and we'll both get $10
buy $100 worth of bitcoin so I get my $10 referral
make sure to send me that Bitcoin

opening.argument: At most, the evidence shows ordinary service promotion and a one-level referral incentive associated with a cryptocurrency exchange. The speaker describes a service that buys and sells digital currency, identifies available payment methods, and mentions a reward for both participants. Nothing supplied shows a guaranteed investment return, a downline or tiered matrix, a required deposit to the speaker, credential harvesting, or a fabricated business. The description presents a Coinbase sign-up link and explains inviting friends, which is consistent with an ordinary referral promotion. The records also do not establish that the stated reward was actually available or paid, so the strongest claims about an operative scam mechanism remain unproven.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A referral promotion and a cryptocurrency purchase are not automatically deceptive. The evidence does not show that viewers were promised guaranteed profits, that recruitment required building a downline, or that funds had to be deposited directly with the speaker. The $10 language identifies a purported ordinary referral benefit, while the Coinbase walkthrough identifies the external service and its payment options. The Bitcoin address alone does not prove what the transfer was for.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The relevant mechanism is not a guaranteed investment return or a tiered matrix; it is compensation dependent on recruited users taking the requested purchase action. The speaker explicitly asks viewers to sign up through the speaker's link, buy $100, and thereby generate the speaker's referral. The additional demand to send Bitcoin makes the solicitation more than neutral explanation of ordinary commerce, even though the records do not prove payment occurred.
